tagline: Across Estill County, a river town between Bluegrass and mountains
intro: Ridgetop Scenic Byway follows Kentucky 89 across Estill County, between the Clark and Jackson county lines. This is the meeting of the Bluegrass and the Cumberland Plateau, where the Kentucky River cuts a deep valley and much of the county’s development occupies its fertile bottomlands. The county’s total relief is nearly 1,000 feet. Kentucky designated Ridgetop Scenic Byway on October 1, 2013.

Irvine’s history reaches back to 1812, when Gen. Green Clay established the town on 20.5 acres of his own land. A century later, the Riverview Hotel was built during a period of oil exploration in the area.

Traveling from the Clark County line toward Jackson County takes you through Irvine, where the historic business district lies roughly at the junction of Kentucky 52 and Kentucky 89. Irvine occupies the northeast side of the Kentucky River; the designated corridor continues to the Jackson County line.

moments.title: Irvine Historic Business District
moments.text: The business district gathers several generations of public and commercial buildings near the meeting of Kentucky 52 and Kentucky 89. Its National Register listing dates to 2000 and included 28 contributing buildings, along with four non-contributing buildings and sites. The district includes the Estill County Courthouse, the Wallace Hotel on Court Street and the Mack Theatre on Main.

moments.title: Riverview Hotel
moments.text: The Riverview Hotel on Main Street is a three-story brick building set on a stone foundation. It was built sometime between 1913 and 1918, during a period of oil exploration in the area. Its Classical Revival architecture and National Register listing, granted in 1992, distinguish this hotel as a historic building.

moments.title: Irvine
moments.text: Irvine began as a town on land belonging to Gen. Green Clay, who established it on January 28, 1812. The post office followed in 1813, but incorporation came later, in 1849. The county seat sits on the northeast side of the Kentucky River, with Ravenna bordering it to the southeast. The county had been created four years before the town, and Irvine later became a summer resort destination. Estill Springs stood near mineral springs in Irvine and attracted 19th-century visitors including Henry Clay, John Crittenden and John C. Breckinridge.
